q7.answer: Presence lives in Redis (shared by all nodes), per connection rather than per user: sorted set pexp:{doc} with member userId|connId and score = expiry time, plus hash cur:{doc} (connId -> latest cursor) and counter pseq:{doc}. Each node's 10 s heartbeat (ZADD XX) pushes expiry to now+30 s and renews the 60 s EXPIRE on the keys; clean leave or sweep removes entries. Per-user grouping is derived by checking for other live members with the same userId.

q8.answer: Nothing is cleaned up by the dead node. Its members stop being renewed, so their scores pass into the past within 30 s. Every surviving node with local sockets on that doc runs the atomic sweep script every 5 s, which removes expired members and their cursors and publishes a leave (last=true when the user has no live connection left) on pres:{doc}. Nodes forward it to their clients; because the script is atomic, only one node publishes each removal. Worst case is about 35 s. If no node has a socket on the doc, the 60 s key EXPIRE clears it.

q9.answer: The sender's node drops updates under 50 ms after the last accepted one, otherwise runs the cursor Lua script, which stores the cursor in cur:{doc} (only if n is higher) and PUBLISHes it on pres:{doc}. Every node subscribed to that channel receives it from Redis and forwards it to its local sockets. The sender's own node is no different: it also receives the event from Redis, not via a local shortcut, so all viewers get the same ordered feed.

q10.answer: The node subscribes to pres:{doc} before running join, so nothing falls between snapshot and live feed. The join script returns the snapshot (users, stored cursors, seq = pseq after this join) atomically with its own publish. The client drops join/leave events with seq <= snapshot.seq as already included. Cursor events are handled by the per-connection counter n and lastN, so a replayed or older cursor is ignored.

q11.answer: Each connection's latest cursor stays in the Redis hash cur:{doc}, even when it is not moving, and the join snapshot includes all stored cursors with rev, n and pos. The joiner holds a cursor whose rev is ahead of its appliedRev, or transforms it forward with transformPosition if older (dropping it on HistoryGone, until the sender's next update).

q12.answer: Each connection stamps cursors with a counter n that only increases. The receiver keeps lastN[connId] and ignores any cursor with n <= lastN, which covers late, duplicate and out-of-order messages and also a held cursor being replaced by a newer one. Redis applies the same rule to the stored cursor, and cursors from a connId that has already left are ignored.
